questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a 5 week history of attacks of pain in the right side of his lower jaw. Brushing his teeth sets off a jolt 'like an electric shock' that lasts a few seconds, then stops completely. He now avoids brushing that side. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. Dental and neurological examinations are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Brief, unilateral, electric-shock pain in a trigeminal distribution triggered by an innocuous stimulus with a normal examination is trigeminal neuralgia.

clues: Brushing his teeth sets off a jolt
Dental and neurological examinations are normal
steps.x: Seconds-long electric shocks in the jaw triggered by tooth brushing, with a normal exam.

elim: Orbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes with tearing and restlessness.
Constant throbbing pain with a tender tooth and swelling; dental exam is normal.
Constant temple pain, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication, not seconds-long shocks.
Aching jaw pain with clicking, worse with prolonged chewing.

steps.x: E: Trigeminal neuralgia. Brief, unilateral, triggered electric-shock facial pain = trigeminal neuralgia.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has a 2 month history of stabbing pains in her left cheek, upper lip and upper teeth. Each lasts a couple of seconds and is set off by touching her face. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Neurological examination, including facial sensation and corneal reflexes, is normal.
questions.q: Which nerve or division is most likely affected?
o: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve
Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
questions.e: The cheek, upper lip and upper teeth are supplied by the maxillary division (V2), one of the two divisions most commonly affected in trigeminal neuralgia.

clues: left cheek, upper lip and upper teeth
steps.x: Map the painful area onto the trigeminal divisions.

elim: The facial nerve is motor to facial muscles; it does not carry facial sensation.
Causes throat and ear pain triggered by swallowing.
Supplies the lower lip, chin and lower teeth.
Supplies the forehead and eye; least often affected.

steps.x: D: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve. Cheek, upper lip and upper teeth = V2, maxillary division.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has a 3 month history of attacks of excruciating pain in his right chin, lower lip and lower teeth. Each lasts 1 to 2 seconds and comes on when he talks or eats. Between attacks he is pain free. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which nerve or division is most likely affected?
o: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve
Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
questions.e: The chin, lower lip and lower teeth are supplied by the mandibular division (V3), commonly affected in trigeminal neuralgia along with V2.

clues: right chin, lower lip and lower teeth
steps.x: Brief shocks in the lower face.

elim: Carries taste from the anterior tongue, not jaw pain.
Causes throat and ear pain triggered by swallowing.
Supplies the cheek, upper lip and upper teeth.
Supplies the forehead and eye.

steps.x: C: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Chin, lower lip and lower teeth = V3, mandibular division.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has trigeminal neuralgia affecting her left cheek. She has attacks of severe, seconds-long stabbing pain several times a day. She covers the left side of her face with a scarf when she goes outside. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely trigger of her attacks?
questions.e: Attacks of trigeminal neuralgia are triggered by innocuous stimuli to the face such as light touch, chewing, brushing teeth or cold wind, which is why she covers her face.

clues: covers the left side of her face with a scarf when she goes outside
steps.x: She protects her face from something outdoors.

elim: A trigger for cluster headache attacks.
Photophobia is a feature of migraine.
Worsens raised intracranial pressure headache.
Aggravates migraine.

steps.x: C: Cold wind on her face. Trigeminal neuralgia triggers: light touch, chewing, brushing teeth, cold wind.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is referred with right-sided facial pain for 6 weeks. His GP suspects trigeminal neuralgia. He has no rash, no nasal or eye symptoms and no history of shingles. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. Facial sensation, corneal reflexes and the rest of the neurological examination are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely description of his pain?
o: Burning pain in an area of previous rash
Severe orbital pain for an hour with tearing
Throbbing pain for a day with nausea
questions.e: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, intermittent, unilateral, electric-shock-like pain lasting only seconds.

steps.x: The question is about the classic pain character.

elim: Describes postherpetic neuralgia; he has no history of shingles.
Trigeminal neuralgia is paroxysmal, not constant.
Describes cluster headache.
Describes migraine.

steps.x: C: Electric-shock pain lasting seconds. Brief, intermittent, unilateral, electric-shock-like, seconds.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has a 3 week history of seconds-long electric-shock pains in her right cheek, triggered by washing her face. She has no other symptoms, no family history of note and takes no medication. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 68 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which feature of her presentation is a red flag for a secondary cause?
o: Pain triggered by washing her face
questions.e: Age under 40 is a red flag because multiple sclerosis can cause trigeminal neuralgia in younger patients; it should prompt investigation rather than assuming idiopathic disease.

steps.x: Everything is typical except the patient herself.

elim: This is expected in idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia.
The classic duration of trigeminal neuralgia.
Innocuous triggers are typical.
Unilateral pain is typical; bilateral pain is the red flag.

steps.x: A: Her age of 35 years. Under 40 = red flag; think multiple sclerosis and investigate.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a 2 month history of brief stabbing pains in his right cheek triggered by chewing. He has also noticed that he has to use his left ear for the telephone. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 134/86 mmHg. Rinne's test is positive bilaterally and Weber's test lateralises to the left.
questions.q: Which feature most warrants further investigation?
o: Reduced hearing in the right ear
questions.e: Deafness is a red flag in trigeminal neuralgia, raising a structural cause such as a cerebellopontine angle tumour; Weber lateralising away from the right with positive Rinne's suggests right sensorineural loss.

clues: use his left ear for the telephone
Weber's test lateralises to the left
steps.x: A hearing deficit on the same side as the pain.

elim: The typical duration of trigeminal neuralgia.
A typical innocuous trigger.
Unilateral pain is typical.
The classic character of trigeminal neuralgia.

steps.x: C: Reduced hearing in the right ear. Red flags: bilateral, visual disturbance, deafness, family history of MS, under 40.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has a 1 month history of electric-shock pains lasting seconds. At first they affected her right cheek, but in the last week she has had identical attacks in her left cheek. They are set off by touching her face. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which feature of her history most strongly suggests a secondary cause?
questions.e: Trigeminal neuralgia is classically unilateral; bilateral symptoms are a red flag for a secondary cause such as multiple sclerosis and should prompt investigation.

clues: identical attacks in her left cheek
At first they affected her right cheek
steps.x: The pain has spread to the other side.

elim: Typical of trigeminal neuralgia.
V2 is one of the most commonly affected divisions.
Expected in idiopathic disease.
A typical innocuous trigger.

steps.x: B: Bilateral symptoms. Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia = red flag for a secondary cause.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has a 2 month history of brief electric-shock pains in his left cheek triggered by shaving. His GP diagnoses idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. The GP then performs a full neurological examination.
questions.q: Which examination finding would make idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia unlikely?
o: Avoidance of touching the left cheek
Reduced sensation over the left cheek
questions.e: Examination in idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia is classically normal; a sensory deficit is a neurological sign that should prompt a search for a secondary cause.

steps.x: The question asks which finding breaks the classic normal exam.

elim: Patients guard trigger zones; this is typical.
Expected in idiopathic disease.
Expected in idiopathic disease.
Expected in idiopathic disease.

steps.x: E: Reduced sensation over the left cheek. Trigeminal neuralgia: normal exam; a deficit means look for a secondary cause.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a 2 month history of attacks of pain in her right cheek and side of her nose, up to 40 times a day. Each lasts 2 to 3 seconds and is triggered by eating. There is no tearing, nasal discharge or rash. Her temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. Sinus tenderness is absent and neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Very brief, frequent, triggered unilateral facial pain without autonomic features and with a normal exam is trigeminal neuralgia; cluster headache lasts much longer with autonomic features.

clues: no tearing, nasal discharge or rash
steps.x: Seconds-long triggered pain, no autonomic features, normal exam.

elim: Constant facial pressure with fever and nasal discharge.
Attacks last 15 to 180 minutes with tearing and nasal discharge.
Pain is provoked by hot, cold or sweet food at a single tooth, not seconds-long shocks.
Follows shingles; there is no rash or history.

steps.x: E: Trigeminal neuralgia. Seconds = trigeminal neuralgia; minutes to hours with tearing = cluster headache.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with trigeminal neuralgia has become drowsy and muddled over 4 days. Her attacks are well controlled. She takes amlodipine, atorvastatin and a drug started 5 weeks ago for her facial pain. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. She is euvolaemic.
questions.q: Which drug is the most likely cause of her investigation results?
questions.e: Carbamazepine, first line for trigeminal neuralgia, commonly causes hyponatraemia (an SIADH-like effect), which explains her confusion 5 weeks after starting it.

clues: drug started 5 weeks ago for her facial pain
steps.x: New confusion with a low sodium after starting a drug for facial pain.

elim: Causes ankle oedema and flushing, not hyponatraemia.
Causes myalgia and raised transaminases.
Not linked with hyponatraemia at normal doses.
Not used for trigeminal neuralgia and does not cause hyponatraemia.

steps.x: C: Carbamazepine. Carbamazepine's common side effect is hyponatraemia.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with trigeminal neuralgia has a positive pregnancy test. She has taken the combined oral contraceptive pill reliably for 10 years without missing a pill. Three months ago she started a new tablet for her facial pain, which has worked well. She takes no other medication. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her contraceptive failure?
questions.e: Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that accelerates metabolism of hormonal contraception, including the COCP, reducing its effectiveness.

clues: taken the combined oral contraceptive pill reliably
started a new tablet for her facial pain
steps.x: Reliable pill use, then a new drug for trigeminal neuralgia.

elim: Gabapentin does not induce liver enzymes and no vomiting is described.
She has taken it reliably.
No diarrhoea is described.
She has used it successfully for 10 years.

steps.x: A: Enzyme induction by carbamazepine. Carbamazepine induces liver enzymes and makes the COCP less effective.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has a 6 week history of seconds-long electric-shock pains in his left upper lip triggered by brushing his teeth. He has no hearing loss, visual symptoms or family history of multiple sclerosis. He asks whether he needs blood tests or a scan. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Trigeminal neuralgia is a clinical diagnosis, which remains the gold standard; with no red flags and a normal examination no test is required.

clues: no hearing loss, visual symptoms or family history of multiple sclerosis
steps.x: Typical older patient with no red flags.

elim: Not needed without red flags and does not confirm the diagnosis.
The pain pattern is neuralgic, not dental.
Used for temporal arteritis, which causes constant temple pain.
Reserved for young patients, atypical features or red flags.

steps.x: A: Clinical history and examination alone. Trigeminal neuralgia: clinical diagnosis is the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has a 2 week history of brief stabbing pains in his left jaw triggered by chewing and talking. He is otherwise well and has no past medical history. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 66 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: In a patient under 40, MRI brain is needed to exclude multiple sclerosis, tumour or structural compression before assuming idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia.

clues: brief stabbing pains in his left jaw
steps.x: Typical trigeminal neuralgia but in a young patient.

elim: The pain is not sinus related.
Used for temporal arteritis in patients over 50.
He is under 40, which is a red flag.
Dental imaging will not exclude a central cause.

steps.x: C: MRI brain. Under 40 or red flags: MRI brain.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has a 1 month history of electric-shock pains in her right forehead and cheek triggered by touch. Over the last week she has noticed blurring of vision in her right eye. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. Visual acuity is reduced on the right. The rest of the neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Visual disturbance is a red flag in trigeminal neuralgia; MRI brain is needed to exclude multiple sclerosis, tumour or structural compression.

clues: blurring of vision in her right eye
Visual acuity is reduced on the right
steps.x: Typical facial pain plus a visual red flag.

elim: A red flag is present, so a secondary cause must be excluded first.
Temporal arteritis causes constant headache and jaw claudication, not shocks.
Visual disturbance is a red flag.
Cannot show demyelination or tumours.

steps.x: C: MRI brain. Visual disturbance with trigeminal neuralgia: MRI brain.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has a 3 week history of brief electric-shock pains in his left cheek triggered by eating. His mother and his sister have multiple sclerosis. He has no visual or hearing symptoms. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Lumbar puncture as the first test
questions.e: A family history of multiple sclerosis is a red flag; MRI brain looks for demyelinating plaques or another structural cause.

clues: His mother and his sister have multiple sclerosis
steps.x: Typical pain, but a family history of MS.

elim: MRI is the first-line imaging; CSF is not the initial test.
Test peripheral nerves, not the trigeminal root entry zone.
A family history of MS is a red flag.
Not the first test for trigeminal neuralgia.

steps.x: B: MRI brain. Family history of MS is a red flag: MRI brain.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman is diagnosed with trigeminal neuralgia and starts carbamazepine. She takes ramipril and indapamide for hypertension. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal. Her GP plans blood tests over the following weeks.
questions.q: Which blood test result is most important to monitor?
questions.e: Hyponatraemia is a common side effect of carbamazepine, and her thiazide-like diuretic and age add to the risk, so sodium must be monitored.

steps.x: A drug that lowers sodium plus a diuretic that also lowers sodium.

elim: Not a recognised carbamazepine problem.
Carbamazepine does not commonly affect glucose.
Not routinely needed for carbamazepine.
No cardiac indication.

steps.x: C: Sodium. Carbamazepine: watch the sodium.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has had trigeminal neuralgia for 3 years. Despite carbamazepine and gabapentin her attacks persist, and she is referred to neurosurgery. She has no history of multiple sclerosis. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal. A high-resolution MRI is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on MRI?
o: Normal brain with no vessel contact
Superior cerebellar artery loop on the nerve root
questions.e: Trigeminal neuralgia is most commonly caused by vascular compression of the nerve root, typically by a loop of the superior cerebellar artery where the nerve enters the pons.

steps.x: Classic idiopathic disease in an older patient without MS.

elim: A secondary cause; less likely with a normal examination.
Would be expected in MS, which she does not have.
Suggests infection or inflammation, not classic neuralgia.
A refractory case referred for surgery usually shows a compressing vessel.

steps.x: E: Superior cerebellar artery loop on the nerve root. Classic trigeminal neuralgia: superior cerebellar artery compressing the root.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has a 1 month history of brief stabbing pains in his right lower jaw triggered by talking. He is diagnosed with trigeminal neuralgia. He has no red flags and takes no medication. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Carbamazepine, an anticonvulsant that inactivates sodium channels, is first line for trigeminal neuralgia; gabapentin is a second-line option.

steps.x: Straightforward diagnosis, first treatment.

elim: Used for other neuropathic pain, not first line for trigeminal neuralgia.
A second-line option if carbamazepine is ineffective or not tolerated.
Steroids do not treat trigeminal neuralgia.
A migraine and cluster headache treatment.

steps.x: B: Carbamazepine. Trigeminal neuralgia first line: carbamazepine.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has trigeminal neuralgia. An MRI brain is normal and she is about to start carbamazepine. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and does not want to become pregnant. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most important advice when starting carbamazepine?
o: Take it only during an attack
questions.e: Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, including the COCP, so she needs a reliable alternative such as a copper IUD.

clues: does not want to become pregnant
steps.x: An enzyme inducer and a hormonal contraceptive.

elim: Grapefruit can interact, but this is not the key risk here.
No such rule applies to trigeminal neuralgia.
Mild drowsiness often settles; it is not the priority.
It is taken regularly, not as needed.

steps.x: E: Use additional or alternative contraception. Carbamazepine plus COCP: advise alternative or additional contraception.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man with trigeminal neuralgia has taken carbamazepine at the maximum tolerated dose for 3 months. His attacks are no less frequent. His sodium and liver tests are normal. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal and an MRI brain shows no secondary cause.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: If carbamazepine is ineffective or not tolerated, second-line options are oxcarbazepine, gabapentin, baclofen or lamotrigine.

steps.x: First line has failed despite an adequate trial.

elim: Not a recommended second-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia.
Opioids are not effective for trigeminal neuralgia.
Steroids have no role.
A migraine and cluster headache treatment.

steps.x: C: Oxcarbazepine. Second line: oxcarbazepine, gabapentin, baclofen or lamotrigine.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with trigeminal neuralgia started carbamazepine 3 weeks ago. Her pain has improved but she has become unsteady and drowsy and has had a fall. Her sodium is normal. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. She has nystagmus on lateral gaze.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Carbamazepine toxicity (ataxia, drowsiness, nystagmus) means it is not tolerated; second-line options include lamotrigine, gabapentin, baclofen or oxcarbazepine.

clues: unsteady and drowsy and has had a fall
steps.x: Carbamazepine is working but not tolerated.

elim: Adds sedation and falls risk.
She is not tolerating carbamazepine; opioids do not help.
Steroids have no role.
Not a treatment for trigeminal neuralgia.

steps.x: C: Lamotrigine. Carbamazepine not tolerated: switch to a second-line drug.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with trigeminal neuralgia has taken carbamazepine for 2 months. He feels nauseated and tired. His attacks were controlled. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. He is euvolaemic and neurological examination is normal. The prescriber decides he cannot continue carbamazepine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Add oral sodium chloride and continue
questions.e: Hyponatraemia is a common side effect of carbamazepine; it should be stopped and a second-line drug such as gabapentin used (oxcarbazepine also lowers sodium).

steps.x: Symptomatic low sodium on carbamazepine.

elim: The cause is the drug; continuing risks worsening hyponatraemia.
Would worsen hyponatraemia.
No role in trigeminal neuralgia.
Not a treatment for trigeminal neuralgia.

steps.x: B: Gabapentin. Carbamazepine hyponatraemia: stop it and use a second-line agent.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man with heart failure and COPD has had trigeminal neuralgia for 5 years. Carbamazepine, gabapentin and baclofen have each failed or caused side effects. His attacks stop him eating. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. Neurological examination and MRI brain are normal. He is not fit for open posterior fossa surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Refractory trigeminal neuralgia needs neurological referral for microvascular decompression or radiofrequency ablation; ablation is the option when he is unfit for open surgery.

clues: each failed or caused side effects
not fit for open posterior fossa surgery
steps.x: Refractory to several drugs and unfit for decompression.

elim: Not an effective treatment for trigeminal neuralgia.
Unsafe; carbamazepine has already failed.
Opioids do not control trigeminal neuralgia.
Not a treatment for trigeminal neuralgia.

steps.x: D: Referral for radiofrequency ablation. Refractory disease: refer for microvascular decompression or radiofrequency ablation.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has a 2 week history of brief electric-shock pains on both sides of her face triggered by touch. She has no other symptoms. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Red flags such as age under 40 or bilateral symptoms need urgent referral for specialist assessment to look for a secondary cause such as multiple sclerosis.

steps.x: Two red flags: young age and bilateral symptoms.

elim: Red flags mean she must not simply be treated as idiopathic.
Second-line drug, and red flags need assessment first.
Two red flags are present.
Surgery is for refractory disease, not first assessment.

steps.x: E: Urgent referral for specialist assessment. Red flag present: urgent specialist referral.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with trigeminal neuralgia has been well on carbamazepine for a year. He now has numbness of his right cheek and upper lip, and his attacks are more frequent. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. Pinprick sensation is reduced over the right maxillary division and the right corneal reflex is reduced.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Add gabapentin and review in 3 months
Reassure that numbness is part of the condition
questions.e: A neurological deficit should prompt consideration of a secondary cause such as a tumour; idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia has a normal examination.

clues: numbness of his right cheek and upper lip
steps.x: A new sensory deficit in someone with known trigeminal neuralgia.

elim: Treats pain but ignores a new neurological deficit.
Ignores the new neurological deficit.
Trigeminal neuralgia classically has a normal examination.

steps.x: D: Refer for a secondary cause. New deficit in trigeminal neuralgia: look for a secondary cause.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has refractory trigeminal neuralgia affecting her left cheek. She undergoes microvascular decompression. The surgeon finds an artery looping around the trigeminal nerve root where it enters the pons and places a pad between them. Afterwards her attacks stop. She has no history of multiple sclerosis.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely to have been compressing the nerve?
questions.e: Trigeminal neuralgia is most often caused by vascular compression of the nerve root, typically a loop of the superior cerebellar artery where the nerve enters the pons.

clues: an artery looping around the trigeminal nerve root where it enters the pons
steps.x: A vessel at the root entry zone at the pons.

elim: Can occasionally be involved but is not the typical vessel.
Lies in the cavernous sinus, not at the root entry zone.
Supplies the lateral cerebral hemisphere.
More often linked with glossopharyngeal neuralgia and lateral medullary syndrome.

steps.x: E: Superior cerebellar artery. Classic culprit: superior cerebellar artery.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man asks why a light breeze on his cheek causes such severe pain. He has trigeminal neuralgia due to a blood vessel pressing on the trigeminal nerve root for many years. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal. Biopsy studies of such nerve roots show a characteristic change.
questions.q: Which change in the nerve root most likely explains his pain?
o: Axonal loss in the trigeminal nucleus
questions.e: Chronic compression causes focal demyelination of the root, which generates ectopic high-frequency firing and ephaptic cross-talk between fibres, so light touch triggers brief severe pain.

clues: light breeze on his cheek causes such severe pain
blood vessel pressing on the trigeminal nerve root for many years
steps.x: Long-standing compression and innocuous stimuli triggering pain.

elim: Would cause numbness, not triggered shocks.
Not the mechanism of compression-related neuralgia.
Causes shingles and postherpetic neuralgia.
Would cause a sensory deficit.

steps.x: B: Focal demyelination. Compression causes focal demyelination, ectopic firing and ephaptic transmission.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis develops brief electric-shock pains in her right cheek triggered by eating. Two years ago she had optic neuritis. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. Neurological examination is otherwise unchanged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her facial pain?
o: Demyelinating plaque at the trigeminal root entry zone
Herpes simplex infection of the ganglion
questions.e: Multiple sclerosis plaques can affect the trigeminal nerve root entry zone, particularly in younger patients, which is why age under 40 is a red flag.

steps.x: A young patient with known MS.

elim: Not linked with MS or this pain pattern.
More typical of diabetic cranial nerve palsies.
The usual cause in older patients without MS.

steps.x: A: Demyelinating plaque at the trigeminal root entry zone. Young plus MS: demyelinating plaque at the root entry zone.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with trigeminal neuralgia asks why an epilepsy drug has stopped her facial pain. She started carbamazepine 3 weeks ago and her attacks have fallen from 30 to 2 a day. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. Her sodium is 137 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the improvement?
o: Reduced ectopic firing through sodium channel blockade
questions.e: Carbamazepine blocks sodium channels, stabilising neuronal membranes and reducing the ectopic firing from the demyelinated root that causes the pain.

clues: epilepsy drug has stopped her facial pain
steps.x: An anticonvulsant controlling neuralgic pain.

elim: The action of baclofen.
The action of SSRIs.
The action of NSAIDs.
The action of opioids, which do not help trigeminal neuralgia.

steps.x: D: Reduced ectopic firing through sodium channel blockade. Carbamazepine: sodium channel block, membrane stabilisation, less ectopic firing.
